levels.title_en: The last two marks, and reading them together

items.pronunciation_notes: Two dots after the letter, read as a light breath echoing the vowel before it. Rare, and confined to Sanskrit-derived vocabulary.

learn.title_en: ः — two dots you will rarely need to write
learn.explanation_en: The visarga is written as two dots after a letter and stands for a light breath that echoes the vowel before it. It belongs almost entirely to Sanskrit-derived vocabulary and has been quietly disappearing from everyday Hindi: दुःख is very often written दुख instead, and both are accepted. Learn to recognise it, but do not expect to need it often.

examples.note: Frequently written दुख without the mark, and said the same way either way.
Formal written Hindi, where the mark closes the word.
Another formal word in which the mark survives.

practice.prompt_en: Add the visarga to this syllable.
practice.question: अत
practice.explanation_en: The visarga is the pair of dots written after the letter, not the single dot above it.

game.explanation_en: The mark is a light breath rather than a full syllable, and the final vowel drops: dukh.

items.pronunciation_notes: The halant has no sound of its own. It cancels the consonant's inherent अ, so क is 'ka' and क् is a bare k.

learn.title_en: ् — the mark that takes a vowel away
learn.explanation_en: Every consonant carries an inherent अ, and the halant cancels it. You will rarely see the mark itself, because when a vowel-less consonant runs into the next consonant the two normally fuse into a single stacked shape instead of showing the halant. So this is less a mark you read than the mechanism behind every conjunct in the levels that follow.

examples.note: Formal register, and one of the few places the mark stays visible.
The halant is not written here — त has already fused with य into a stack.
The commonest word in Hindi built out of a stack.

practice.prompt_en: Remove the inherent vowel from this letter.
practice.question: क
practice.explanation_en: The halant is the small stroke below the letter, and it leaves a bare consonant with no vowel.

game.explanation_en: The halant removes the vowel from क, so the two consonants run together with nothing between them: kyaa.

items.pronunciation_notes: Words routinely carry several marks at once. Read the consonant first, then its matra, then any nasal or other mark attached to it.
items.gloss_en: combined reading of matras and marks

learn.explanation_en: You now have all ten matras plus four other marks, and real words combine them freely. The order in which you read them is fixed even though the order in which they are drawn is not: take the consonant first, then whatever matra belongs to it, then any nasal or other mark. किताबें has a matra drawn before its first consonant and a dot above its last — read in the written order it is nonsense, read in the spoken order it is straightforward.

examples.note: A left-drawn matra, a dot, then a right-drawn matra — three marks in one short word.
The final ब carries both a matra and a dot.
A matra and a crescent sitting on the same syllable.

common_error.why_en: A real n is pronounced before द, so this word takes the plain dot rather than the crescent.

practice.prompt_en: Add both the ि matra and the anusvara to this letter.
practice.question: ह
practice.explanation_en: The short ि goes to the left of the consonant and the plain dot goes above it.

game.explanation_en: The final syllable carries both the े matra and the dot, so the word ends in a nasalised vowel: kitaabeṁ.

summary.recap_en: This level added the visarga and the halant, completing the mark inventory, and practised reading words that carry several marks at once. The halant matters most for what comes next: it is the mechanism behind every conjunct.
summary.next_up_en: Next: how two consonants fuse into a single shape, र's two special forms, and the first of the four conjuncts taught as extra letters.

items.pronunciation_notes: A stack is always read as two consonants with no vowel between them, whatever shape the writing takes.

learn.title_en: How two letters become one shape
learn.explanation_en: When a consonant loses its vowel and runs straight into the next consonant, Hindi normally writes the pair as a single joined shape rather than writing the halant. There are three common ways this happens: the first letter drops its vertical stem and the two sit side by side, as in स्त; the pair stacks vertically, as in न्न; or the two fuse into a shape you simply memorise, as in क्ष. Whichever shape appears, the reading is identical — two consonants, no vowel between them.

examples.note: Two च sounds run together with nothing between them.
त loses its stem and य follows immediately.
Probably the single most-used word in spoken Hindi, and it contains a stack.

common_error.why_en: Writing the two letters separately puts a vowel between them, which is not how the word is said.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: च् + च
practice.explanation_en: The halant on the first letter removes its vowel, and the two fuse into one shape.

game.explanation_en: The stack is च followed by छ, so an unaspirated and then an aspirated sound are both heard: achchhaa.

items.pronunciation_notes: र behaves unlike any other consonant in a stack. Before another consonant it becomes a hook above the line, read BEFORE that consonant; after one it becomes a stroke below, read after it.
items.gloss_en: र in conjuncts — its two special forms

learn.explanation_en: र is the one consonant that does not simply fuse in place. When it comes first in a stack it is written as a small hook above the line, sitting over the letter that follows it but read before it: कर्म is 'karm', not 'krma'. When it comes second it becomes a short stroke attached underneath: प्र is 'pra'. Two shapes, two positions, and in the first case the reading order is the reverse of what your eye suggests.

examples.note: The hook sits over म but is read before it.
र beneath प, and read after it.
The hook sits over य, again read before it.

common_error.why_en: Both are real words, and the position of र is the whole difference: कर्म is 'karm', while क्रम is 'kram', meaning order or sequence.

practice.prompt_en: Build the word in this order: क, then र with no vowel, then म.
practice.question: क + र् + म
practice.explanation_en: र comes before म, so it is written as the hook above म. Written beneath क it would give क्रम, a different word.

game.explanation_en: र sits beneath प and is read after it, so the word opens 'pre' rather than 'per'.

items.pronunciation_notes: क् plus ष, read 'ksh'. The written shape gives no clue about its parts, so it has to be memorised as a unit.

learn.title_en: क्ष — the first of four shapes you memorise
learn.explanation_en: Four conjuncts are so heavily fused that their shapes no longer resemble their parts, and Hindi children learn them as extra letters tacked onto the end of the alphabet. क्ष is the first: it is क् plus ष, read 'ksh'. There is no way to work the shape out by looking at it, so treat it as a single character that happens to carry a two-consonant sound.

examples.note: Used as a formal apology.
The conjunct sitting in the middle of a word.
Very common in news and official writing.

common_error.why_en: Writing the letters separately inserts a vowel between them, and it also uses श where the word takes ष.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: क् + ष
practice.explanation_en: क् and ष fuse into one shape that shows neither part clearly, read 'ksh'.

game.explanation_en: The conjunct runs k straight into sh with no vowel between, and the following vowel is short: kshamaa.

summary.recap_en: This level explained how stacks are built and introduced the one consonant that breaks the pattern. र is written as a hook above the following letter but read before it, which reverses the reading order your eye expects.
summary.next_up_en: Next: त्र, ज्ञ and श्र complete the four conjuncts that are learned as separate letters.

items.pronunciation_notes: त् plus र, read 'tr'. Words ending in this conjunct usually keep their final vowel, so मित्र is 'mitra' rather than 'mitr'.

learn.explanation_en: त्र is त् plus र. Unlike the hook and stroke forms from the last level, this pair has its own fused shape, which is why it is grouped with the conjuncts taught as extra letters. Notice something about its words: मित्र is 'mitra', not 'mitr'. When a conjunct ends in र the final vowel is normally kept, though not every conjunct behaves this way — the last level of this module sorts out which do.

examples.note: Formal register; दोस्त is the everyday word.
The final vowel is pronounced, because a conjunct comes before it.
You will see this on tickets and station signs everywhere.

common_error.why_en: Writing the letters separately puts a vowel between them; the conjunct runs त straight into र.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: त् + र
practice.explanation_en: त् plus र gives त्र. Reversed, र् plus त would put the hook above the line instead.

game.explanation_en: This conjunct keeps the final vowel that would normally drop, so the word ends in a: mitra.

items.pronunciation_notes: Written as ज् plus ञ, but standard Hindi pronounces it 'gy'. The written parts and the spoken sound simply do not match.

learn.title_en: ज्ञ — written one way, said another
learn.explanation_en: ज्ञ is the strangest of the four. Its parts are ज् and ञ, so by the ordinary rules it ought to read 'jny', and in Sanskrit recitation it sometimes still does. Standard Hindi says 'gy' instead. Nothing in the shape tells you this, so it has to be learned as a plain fact about the letter rather than derived from anything.

examples.note: Formal, but common in writing and in speeches.
You will meet this in any school or news context.
Common in newspapers and on hoardings.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: ज् + ञ
practice.explanation_en: ज् plus ञ gives ज्ञ, and standard Hindi reads that shape as 'gy' despite its parts.

game.explanation_en: The conjunct is written from ज and ञ but pronounced 'gy', so the word is vigyaan.

items.pronunciation_notes: श् plus र, read 'shr'. The most transparent of the four — both parts are still visible in the shape.

example_word.english: Mr; an honorific placed before a name

learn.title_en: श्र — the last of the four
learn.explanation_en: श्र is श् plus र, and it is the most predictable of the four special conjuncts, since the shape still shows both parts. It earns its place in the group by frequency rather than difficulty: श्री is the standard honorific placed before a man's name in formal writing and speech, so you will meet this conjunct constantly on documents, signs and envelopes.

examples.note: Placed before a name in formal writing and address.
Formal vocabulary, common in official language.
Borrowed into English in almost this exact form.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: श् + र
practice.explanation_en: श् plus र gives श्र, with र written as a stroke beneath the first letter.

game.explanation_en: र attaches beneath श and is read after it, and the final vowel drops: aashram.

summary.recap_en: This level completed the four conjuncts that Hindi teaches as extra letters. क्ष and ज्ञ have to be memorised outright, ज्ञ because its sound contradicts its parts, while त्र and श्र still show what they are made of.
summary.next_up_en: Next: ordinary stacks, starting with the half-form pattern that makes most conjuncts readable at sight.

items.pronunciation_notes: स loses its vertical stem and त follows immediately. The two consonants run together with no vowel between them.

learn.explanation_en: Most conjuncts are far more transparent than the four you have just learned. The commonest pattern is the half-form: the first letter loses its vertical stem and the second is written straight after it. स्त is exactly that — स without its stem, then त. Once you can spot a missing stem, a large number of conjuncts become readable on sight without any memorising at all.

examples.note: You will use this every time you ask for directions.
The everyday word, where मित्र from the last level is the formal one.
The greeting everyone knows, and it contains this stack.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: स् + त
practice.explanation_en: स drops its vertical stem and त is written immediately after it.

game.explanation_en: The first vowel is long and the stack runs स straight into त with nothing between: raastaa.

items.pronunciation_notes: द् above ध in a vertical stack. Both consonants are pronounced — the sound is held slightly longer and then released with breath.

learn.title_en: द्ध — a stack you have to hold twice
learn.explanation_en: द्ध is द् plus ध: a plain voiced dental followed immediately by its breathy partner. Both are genuinely pronounced, so the consonant is held a little longer and then released with breath. English speakers tend to produce only one of the two, which makes शुद्ध come out as 'shudh'. This one stacks vertically rather than using a half-form, so the first letter sits above the second.

examples.note: You will see this on food packaging constantly.
Common in news writing and headlines.
Related to बुद्धि, meaning intelligence.

common_error.why_en: Only one consonant is written here, but two are pronounced — a plain द and then a breathy ध.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: द् + ध
practice.explanation_en: द् sits above ध in a vertical stack, and both consonants are sounded.

game.explanation_en: Both consonants of the stack are heard, and unlike मित्र this word drops its final vowel: yuddh.

items.pronunciation_notes: न् stacked above न. The n is genuinely held for longer than a single letter, not merely written twice.

learn.explanation_en: Doubled consonants are common in Hindi, and they are genuinely held longer rather than just written twice. न्न is न् above न, and the n lasts noticeably longer than a single one would. English only does this across a word boundary, as in 'thin nail', so holding the sound inside a single word is a habit that has to be built on purpose.

examples.note: The final vowel drops, so the word ends on the held n.
Formal register, common in written Hindi.
Two stacks in one word — प्र at the front and न्न at the end.

common_error.why_en: A single न gives a short sound; the stack holds it noticeably longer, and the two are different words.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: न् + न
practice.explanation_en: न् stacks above न, and the resulting n is held longer than a single letter would be.

game.explanation_en: Both न letters are pronounced, holding the n longer, and the final vowel drops: bhinn.

summary.recap_en: This level began the ordinary stacks with स्त, द्ध and न्न, covering both written patterns: the half-form, where the first letter loses its stem, and the vertical stack, where it sits on top of the second.
summary.next_up_en: Next: nine more common stacks, and then the level that decides which written vowels are actually pronounced.
